# The ESCO claim, audited against ESCO

*Run 2026-10-04. Every figure here is regenerated by `week 4/esco_audit.py`.*

The ESCO section is the only part of this study whose central claim is about an
**object outside our own data**. Every other finding asks the reader to trust a
corpus they cannot see. *"ESCO has no concept for Kubernetes"* can be checked in
ten seconds by typing Kubernetes into ESCO's search box — so a single wrong
example costs more credibility than the section buys.

This is that check, done before publication rather than after.

---

## The short version

**The central claim survives, and it survives in a form that is checkable.** But
three things in the current write-up are wrong as stated, one of them in the way
that gets noticed first, and the claim has to be narrowed from *ESCO* to *ESCO's
skills pillar*.

| | published | audited |
|---|---|---|
| anchor set | "14,359 defined skill concepts" | **13,939 skills + 420 category headings** |
| ESCO version | not stated in the article | **v1.2.0, May 2024** — v1.2.1 exists (Dec 2025) |
| what was searched | "ESCO" | **the skills pillar only** |
| residual | 26.4% | 26.4% published · **25.3%** net of retrieval misses · **35.3%** if headings do not count |

---

## 1. The part that holds, and why it is worth defending

The headline rests on modern software tooling having no ESCO concept. Checked by
plain string search over all 214,482 labels we anchored against — no embeddings,
so the result is reproducible by anyone with the download:

**Genuinely absent from ESCO v1.2.0:** Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Power BI,
Spring Boot, Databricks, Kafka, GraphQL, Snowflake, Salesforce, REST APIs,
microservices, CI/CD, ISO 27001, prompt engineering, large language models,
back-end, B2B, account management, driving licence.

Three apparent hits are substring artefacts and must not be quoted as coverage:
`azure` matches *keramische glazuren*, `aws` matches *gaming laws*, `react`
matches *thermic reaction processes*, `tableau` matches French *tableaux de
charge*. ESCO does **not** carry Azure, AWS or React.

**The method's own failure story is the strongest thing in the section.** Pure
cosine anchoring returned a residual of exactly 0.0% — every group matched
something — and the matches were polysemous: `Sound judgment` → *set up sound
equipment*, `SonarQube` → *assist in ship manoeuvring*, `Spring Boot` → *oversee
spring making machine*. A wrong match scored 0.148 on distinctiveness where a
right one scored 0.151. That is a real negative result, honestly reported, and
it is why the shortlist-plus-judgement design exists.

**The asymmetry Hypothesis 2 predicted survives every variant tested**, including
the strictest. Under the rule that a category heading does not count as
coverage: software's residual is 17.1% novelty against sales' 8.4%, and sales'
is 16.7% vagueness against software's 11.0%. Same direction, and it is the
direction rather than the totals that H2 claimed.

---

## 2. What is wrong and must change before publication

### 2.1 The concept count does not match ESCO's own

We say **14,359 defined skill concepts**. ESCO publishes **13,939**, and that is
the number a reader will find.

Both are right about different things. Under `/esco/skill/` the distribution
holds 15,163 concepts; 804 are marked obsolete and were correctly excluded,
leaving 14,359. Of those, **13,939 carry `rdf:type esco:Skill`** and **420 carry
no type at all** — they are the headings that organise the pillar, such as
*communication skills*. We loaded both and counted both as skills.

**Fix:** state it as *13,939 skills, plus 420 hierarchy headings also used as
anchor targets*. The audit script asserts on 13,939 so this cannot drift again.

### 2.2 Twenty-six anchors rest on a heading, not a skill

26 of 424 anchored clusters (**6.1%**) matched a heading rather than a concept —
`Communication skills` → *communication skills*, `Interpersonal skills` →
*interpersonal skills*, `General skills` → *Kernfähigkeiten und -kompetenzen*.
Fifteen are transversal-skills headings, eleven are skills-hierarchy headings.

Whether that is coverage is a judgement, not a fact. ESCO does publish these as
concepts with URIs, so *"ESCO has no concept for communication skills"* would be
false and easily disproven — which is why the published, looser treatment is the
right default. But it is a judgement that moves the number a long way:

| | overall | software | sales |
|---|---|---|---|
| a heading counts as coverage (published) | 26.4% | 27.5% | 24.4% |
| only a specific skill counts | **35.3%** | 34.8% | **36.3%** |

⚠️ **The order of the two families reverses.** Published, software's residual is
larger; under the strict rule, sales' is. The article leans on composition
rather than totals, so H2 is unaffected — but any sentence comparing the two
*totals* must not be written as if the comparison were robust.

### 2.3 Nine clusters are in the residual although ESCO plainly carries them

This is the item that would do the damage, because each one is a ten-second
check against ESCO's search box.

| cluster | our label | ESCO's label | atoms |
|---|---|---|---|
| 608 | Interpersonal skills | *interpersonal skills* | 1,253 |
| 211 | Information security | *information security* | 466 |
| 549 | Communication skills | *communication skills* | 432 |
| 546 | GCP/GDPR knowledge | *knowledge of GDPR* | 522 |
| 603 | DevOps practices | *DevOps* | 394 |
| 471 | Adobe Creative Suite | *Adobe Creative Suite* | 241 |
| 391, 8 | Data analysis | *data analysis* | 348 |
| 82 | Writing skills | *writing skills* | 152 |

**The cause is retrieval, not judgement.** The shortlist is the top five by
cosine between a cluster *centroid* — the average of a few hundred multilingual
member phrases — and an ESCO label. When the centroid drifts from the concept's
exact wording, the right concept never enters the five, and the adjudicator is
asked to choose among five wrong answers. It answered `null`, correctly. Cluster
549 `Communication skills` was offered *"Klären, wie verschiedene Komponenten
zusammenarbeiten"* at 0.712 while ESCO holds the literal string.

Worth **1.09 points**: the residual falls 26.4% → **25.3%**, software 27.5% →
26.3%, sales 24.4% → 23.5%. Direction unchanged.

⚠️ **A first pass put this at 6%, and the number was an artefact.** The sweep
accepted a match on *any* member phrase, so `Microsoft Azure` came back "in
ESCO" because one member reads *Microsoft Access*, and `PowerPoint proficiency`
because one reads *PowerShell*. Reading the members cut it from 23 clusters to
9. Third time in this project that a category produced a striking number and the
members disowned it.

### 2.4 Only one of ESCO's pillars was ever searched

ESCO has occupations, skills and qualifications. **Only skills were downloaded**,
and the write-up says so in week 2 — but the article says "ESCO" and "Europe's
own list of skills", which reads as all of it.

* **credentials are 11.8% of the residual.** `Bachelor's degree`,
  `Comparable qualification`, `Mathematics degree`. ESCO keeps qualifications in
  a separate pillar that was never searched;
* **availability is 1.7%**, and ESCO genuinely does not model it as a skill;
* **cluster 616 `Trade occupation experience`** holds German trades —
  *Schreiner*, *Zimmermann*, *Maurer*. ESCO carries those as **occupations**.
  "No ESCO concept" is true of the skills pillar and false of ESCO.

Excluding credentials and availability the residual is **25.1%**.

**Fix:** every statement becomes *"no concept in ESCO's skills pillar"*. The
claim is still interesting — employers write requirements the skills taxonomy
cannot express — and it is no longer overstated.

### 2.5 The version is not stated, and a newer one exists

We used **v1.2.0 (May 2024)**. ESCO released **v1.2.1 in December 2025**, a
minor update. Pinning the version is standard and already the module's stated
intention — "concepts are added between releases, so the residual is
version-sensitive. Pin it and print it" — but the article never prints it.

Not a defect in the result; a defect in the write-up. Novelty claims about a
taxonomy are meaningless without the version and date beside them.

### 2.6 Two smaller things, both free to fix

**Atoms in no cluster count as covered.** 5,729 atoms (**1.64%**) are HDBSCAN
noise or unmatched, so they carry no ESCO decision at all — yet the test is
`cluster in unanchored`, which is False for them, and they land on the covered
side. Measured over clustered atoms only, the residual is **26.9%** rather than
26.4%.

**Six of 28 languages.** ESCO publishes 28; we loaded en, de, fr, it, es, nl —
214,482 labels. That covers 81.0% of atoms by advert language; **3.8% are in a
named language with no ESCO labels loaded** (Swedish, Portuguese, Polish, Danish,
Lithuanian, Romanian, Bulgarian) and 15.2% have the field empty. Clusters are
multilingual — no cluster of 617 exceeds 90% one language — so the effect is
diluted rather than absent, and it pushes the residual **up**.

---

## 3. The hole that no amount of re-reading closes

**There is no measured error rate on the adjudication.** 617 decisions were made
by a model. 25 were checked by hand, and they were deliberately drawn from the
suspicious cases — which is the right way to find failure modes and the wrong
way to estimate a rate.

A random sample of 40 (`week 3/review_sets.json`, set D8, drawn 2026-09-14,
seeded) exists precisely to fix this, and **was never labelled**. Until it is,
the honest formulation is *617 model judgements, spot-checked* — not *measured*.

Everything else in this audit is a correction to a number. This one is a
missing instrument, and it is the cheapest of all of them: forty rows, each a
cluster name, five candidates and a yes/no.

---

## 4. What to change, in order

1. ✅ **State the version and the pillar.** "ESCO v1.2.0 (May 2024), skills
   pillar" wherever the claim appears. Done in the article and the figure.
2. ✅ **Correct the concept count** to 13,939 skills plus 420 headings. Done,
   and `esco_audit.py` now asserts on 13,939 so it cannot drift back.
3. ✅ **Re-run the shortlist with a lexical channel.** Done — see §6.
4. ❌ **Label the 40 random decisions.** Decided against on 2026-10-04. The
   published wording is therefore *617 model judgements, spot-checked*, never
   *measured*. §6 supplies a reproducibility figure, which is a different thing
   and must not be presented as an accuracy figure.
5. ✅ **Report the heading sensitivity** as a band: 26.4% published, 35.3%
   strict. In the article as a warning against comparing the two totals.
6. ⬜ **Decide the noise atoms** — 1.64% of atoms are in no cluster, carry no
   ESCO decision, and count as covered. Still neither excluded nor declared.

---

## 5. The sentence the evidence supports

> Roughly a quarter of what European employers ask for — **26% to 29% of
> requirement mass** — has no matching concept in the skills pillar of ESCO
> v1.2.0. The gap is not evenly shaped: software's leans to tools the catalogue
> has not caught up with (Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Databricks, Spring
> Boot, prompt engineering, none of which ESCO contains), sales' to requirements
> too vague to name.

That is narrower than "a quarter of what employers ask for has no name in
Europe's skills list", and it is the version that holds up when someone opens
ESCO and checks.

---

## 6. The repair, and the thing it uncovered

*Run 2026-10-04. `week 4/esco_reanchor.py`, `esco_stability.py`,
`esco_consolidate.py`.*

### What was built

`esco_adjudicate.lexical_candidates` puts an exact-label hit on the ballot
beside the five cosine candidates, so the adjudicator can no longer be asked to
choose among five wrong answers when ESCO holds the concept verbatim. Exact
match only — a fuzzy channel would re-import the polysemy that made cosine
unusable in the first place.

⚠️ **The first version of the fix was itself a defect.** It filled to a fixed
ballot of five, so two literal candidates displaced the two weakest cosine
picks and a group whose right answer sat fifth lost it. `k` now counts cosine
picks only. Correcting it changed almost nothing — 87 groups moved before and
87 after — which is what sent the investigation to the control below.

### The thing it uncovered: the adjudicator does not agree with itself

Asking the **identical question twice**, same prompt, same candidates, fresh
cache:

| | |
|---|---|
| agreement on anchored-or-not | **90.8%** — 57 of 617 groups flip |
| agreement on *which* ESCO concept | **54.0%** |
| residual mass, run 1 against run 2 | 26.44% against **25.75%** |

**Per-group decisions are noisy; the aggregate is not.** That distinction is the
whole result. The cluster dictionary's ESCO column should not be read as a
settled fact about any one group, and the residual percentage is reproducible to
about a point.

Nobody had asked this question before. It is a larger source of error than the
retrieval defect that prompted the audit, and it was invisible because the first
run was cached and never repeated.

### The published number, from three draws

The final procedure was drawn three times and each group takes the majority.

| draw | overall | software | sales |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 26.83% | 25.91% | 28.66% |
| 2 | 28.23% | 28.19% | 28.33% |
| 3 | 25.89% | 25.81% | 26.04% |
| **majority** | **27.49%** | **26.81%** | **28.85%** |

92.1% of groups get the same verdict in all three; **8.0% of requirement mass**
sits in the groups they disagree about. Quote the figure as a band.

### Two corrections, pulling in opposite directions

Nine groups came **out** of the residual because ESCO holds them and the
shortlist had never offered them. More went **in**, because three draws reject
anchors that one draw accepted — and reading those is what settles whether the
rise is an improvement:

| group | what the first run had matched it to |
|---|---|
| `REST API experience` | *cera d'api* — beeswax, in Italian |
| `Infrastructure as code (Terraform)` | *infrastructuur beheren* |
| `Willingness to relocate or travel` | *fare ampi e numerosi viaggi internazionali* |
| `Full-stack development` | *apply basic programming skills* |

These are the "closeness is not sameness" failures the design exists to catch,
and the published run let them through. **The residual rose because the
instrument got stricter.**

### What this does to Hypothesis 2

The direction survives; the magnitude does not.

| | first run | audited, majority of three |
|---|---|---|
| software novelty vs sales | 5.7 vs 2.9 — **2.0×** | 6.7 vs 5.1 — **1.3×** |
| sales vagueness vs software | 7.3 vs 4.5 — 1.6× | 5.7 vs 3.5 — **1.6×** |
| which family's total is larger | software | **sales** |

"Software's residual is novelty at twice sales' rate" was true of one draw of a
procedure with a known retrieval defect. It is not true now. The vagueness
asymmetry is unchanged, and which family carries the larger total was never
robust — §2.2 already showed it reversing on the heading question alone.
